claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3A and associated videos.

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in explanted healthy guts did not show major changes in their GFP levels, indicative of continuous esg expression.
claims.source: Progenitor cells in explanted healthy guts did not show major changes in their GFP levels, indicative of continuous esg expression, nor in their nuclear size (Figure 3D, F and G and Figure 3—video 4), which indicates that DNA content remains constant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3D, F, and G.

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in explanted healthy guts did not show major changes in their nuclear size, which indicates that DNA content remains constant.
claims.source: Progenitor cells in explanted healthy guts did not show major changes in their GFP levels, indicative of continuous esg expression, nor in their nuclear size (Figure 3D, F and G and Figure 3—video 4), which indicates that DNA content remains constant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3D, F, and G.

claims.claim: GFP-labeled progenitor cells did not divide in healthy explanted intestines.
claims.source: Via cell tracking we also observed that GFP-labeled progenitor cells did not divide in healthy explanted intestines (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: In healthy explanted intestines, cell death or enterocyte (EC) extrusion events were not observed until after 48–72 hr of culture.
claims.source: It is important to note that in said healthy intestines we did not observe cell death or enterocyte (EC) extrusion events until after 48–72 hr of culture.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Healthy enterocytes are known to suppress ISC proliferation.
claims.source: As healthy enterocytes are known to suppress ISC proliferation (Liang et al., 2017), this may explain the lack of cell division in our explants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The suppression of peristaltic movements by isradipine may prevent EC loss by reducing mechanical tissue stress.
claims.source: The suppression of peristaltic movements by isradipine may also prevent EC loss by reducing mechanical tissue stress (Li et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: ISC proliferation events could be detected in SDS-damaged intestines.
claims.source: ISC proliferation events could also be detected (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: ISC mitoses could generally be observed only in cases where tissue damage was extensive.
claims.source: However, ISC mitoses could generally be observed only in cases where tissue damage was extensive, as evidenced by the appearance of pyknotic or fragmented nuclei and the extrusion of multiple (>3) contiguous ECs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Many progenitor cells could be observed growing in nuclear size while simultaneously losing GFP expression, indicative of differentiation events towards the EC identity.
claims.source: In addition to ISC divisions, many progenitor cells could be observed growing in nuclear size while simultaneously losing GFP expression (Figure 3B and E–G and Figure 3—video 3, Figure 3—video 4) indicative of differentiation events towards the EC identity.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3B, E-G and associated videos.

claims.claim: Differentiating progenitor cells could be seen replacing dying enterocytes.
claims.source: Indeed, differentiating progenitor cells could be seen replacing dying enterocytes (Figure 3—video 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—video 3.

claims.claim: After SDS feeding, several esg+ cells with larger nuclei were observed.
claims.source: After SDS feeding, we observed several esg + cells with larger nuclei (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B.

claims.claim: At later time-points after SDS treatment, many differentiating cells with large nuclei and low GFP expression were present.
claims.source: At later time-points many differentiating cells with large nuclei and low GFP expression were also present, similarl to what was observed ex vivo.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Proliferative cells could be found almost exclusively at 48 hr after the end of the SDS treatment.
claims.source: Moreover, similarly to explanted midguts, proliferative cells could be found almost exclusively at 48 hr after the end of the SDS treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Progenitor cells could be observed both dividing and differentiating in response to wounding with a tungsten needle.
claims.source: Similarly to the SDS damage protocol, we were able to record progenitor cells both dividing and differentiating (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C and Figure 3—video 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, C and Figure 3—video 5.

claims.claim: Wounding stimulated the robust expression of the cytokine Unpaired 3 (Upd3).
claims.source: Moreover, wounding stimulated the robust expression of the cytokine Unpaired 3 (Upd3), whose function in midgut damage response is well documented (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E and Figure 3—video 6; Figure 3—video 7; Jiang et al., 2009; Patel et al., 2015; Buchon et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D, E and associated videos, as well as citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Both ISCs and EBs are quiescent in undamaged intestines.
claims.source: All in all, our observations suggest that both ISCs and EBs are quiescent in undamaged intestines.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Previous studies showed varying rates of ISC proliferation in healthy midguts in vivo.
claims.source: While previous studies did show varying rates of ISC proliferation in healthy midguts in vivo (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Jiang et al., 2009; Reiff et al., 2019; de Navascués et al., 2012), this may be attributed to cell death (Liang et al., 2017) as well as the passage of food through the intestinal lumen (Li et al., 2018), both of which do not occur in our midgut cultures until later time-points (i.e. after 48–72 hr).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Several previous studies used lineage-tracing tools requiring a 37 °C heat shock for their activation, a treatment known to induce ISC proliferation.
claims.source: Moreover, several previous studies used lineage-tracing tools requiring a 37 °C heat shock for their activation, a treatment known to induce ISC proliferation (Beebe et al., 2010; de Navascués et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2008; Shaw et al., 2010; Strand and Micchelli, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claims.claim: In the presence of tissue damage, progenitor cells could be robustly activated in explanted intestines.
claims.source: Indeed, in the presence of tissue damage, progenitor cells could be robustly activated in explanted intestines, indicating that both ISCs and EBs are capable of responding to their environment after organ explant.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: The Delta/Notch signaling that occurs between ISCs and adjacent EBs is a key pathway necessary for progenitor cell differentiation.
claims.source: A key pathway necessary for progenitor cell differentiation is the Delta/Notch signaling that occurs between ISCs and adjacent EBs (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: The depletion of Notch (N) by RNA interference (NRNAi) in esg+ cells has been shown to promote the formation of undifferentiated tumor-like masses in vivo.
claims.source: The depletion of Notch (N) by RNA interference (NRNAi) in esg+ cells has been shown to promote the formation of undifferentiated tumor-like masses in vivo (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Patel et al., 2015; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Tumor initiation by N-depleted ISCs requires proliferation induced by tissue stress.
claims.source: Notably, tumor initiation by N-depleted ISCs requires proliferation induced by tissue stress (Patel et al., 2015; Apidianakis et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: When midguts from flies expressing NRNAi in progenitor cells for 24 h prior to dissection were cultured for 48 hr, tumorigenesis was not observed in the absence of tissue damage.
claims.source: Consistent with this, when we explanted midguts from flies expressing NRNAi in progenitor cells for 24 h prior to dissection and cultured them for 48 hr, we did not observe tumorigenesis in the absence of tissue damage (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—video 8).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and Figure 3—video 8.

claims.claim: When guts expressing NRNAi were accidentally damaged during dissection, esg+ cells started to proliferate.
claims.source: However, when guts were accidentally damaged during dissection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, yellow ellipses), esg+ cells started to proliferate (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B, yellow squares, and Figure 3—video 9).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and Figure 3—video 9.

claims.claim: Progenitor cells expressing NRNAi remained small and did not lose GFP expression, suggesting a block of differentiation ex vivo in response to Notch knock-down.
claims.source: Notably, progenitor cells remained small and did not lose GFP expression (compare Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B as well as Figure 3—video 2 and Figure 3—video 9), suggesting a block of differentiation ex vivo in response to Notch knock-down.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B and Figure 3—video 9.

claims.claim: EGFR-Ras-Erk signaling is activated upon gut tissue damage.
claims.source: EGFR-Ras-Erk signaling is activated upon gut tissue damage, and this pathway is required for stem cell activation in the adult Drosophila intestine (Buchon et al., 2010; Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Jiang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: EGFR-Ras-Erk signaling is required for stem cell activation in the adult Drosophila intestine.
claims.source: EGFR-Ras-Erk signaling is activated upon gut tissue damage, and this pathway is required for stem cell activation in the adult Drosophila intestine (Buchon et al., 2010; Biteau and Jasper, 2011; Jiang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Expression of a constitutively active form of Ras (RasG12V) strongly promotes stem cell proliferation in adult midguts.
claims.source: Previous experiments showed that expression of a constitutively active form of Ras (RasG12V) strongly promotes stem cell proliferation in adult midguts (Jiang et al., 2011; Jin et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: When RasG12V was induced in explanted midguts using the esgTS driver, progenitor cells started to rapidly proliferate.
claims.source: When explanted midguts were shifted to the permissive temperature (29 °C) at the start of imaging, progenitor cells, marked by GFP co-expressed with RasG12V, started to rapidly proliferate (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: About 20% of progenitor cells tracked from the moment they expressed visible amounts of GFP till the end of the imaging session were seen proliferating after RasG12V expression.
claims.source: About 20% of progenitor cells tracked from the moment they expressed visible amounts of GFP till the end of the imaging session, were seen proliferating (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: As GFP+ cells accumulated in the tissue after RasG12V expression, enterocytes were displaced and extruded from the epithelium.
claims.source: As GFP+ cells accumulated in the tissue, enterocytes were displaced and extruded from the epithelium (Figure 4B, yellow arrowhead, and Figure 4—video 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—video 2.

claims.claim: Some GFP+ progenitor cells expressing RasG12V did not proliferate, but their nuclei rapidly grew in size, which aligns with the previously reported role of EGFR signaling in promoting EB growth.
claims.source: Interestingly, some GFP+ progenitor cells did not proliferate, but their nuclei rapidly grew in size, which aligns with the previously reported role of EGFR signaling in promoting EB growth (Jiang et al., 2011; Xiang et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Rapidly growing progenitors expressing RasG12V also lost GFP expression during the course of imaging, which suggests their differentiation towards the EC lineage.
claims.source: Moreover, these rapidly growing progenitors also lost GFP expression during the course of imaging, which suggests their differentiation towards the EC lineage.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: The extended live-imaging that the protocol allows permitted following cells through multiple rounds of mitosis.
claims.source: The extended live-imaging that our protocol allows also permitted us to follow cells through multiple rounds of mitosis.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Using manual 3-dimensional (3D) cell tracking, the lineages of 17 dividing cells that expressed RasG12V were reconstructed.
claims.source: Using manual 3-dimensional (3D) cell tracking, we reconstructed the lineages of 17 dividing cells that expressed RasG12V (see Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1 for an example).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—video 1.

claims.claim: ISCs are the only cell type in the Drosophila intestine that normally divide multiple times.
claims.source: As ISCs are the only cell type in the Drosophila intestine that normally divide multiple times (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006; Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Chen et al., 2018), the founding cells in these lineages were most likely ISCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: A recent work suggested that RasG12V can push a small number of EBs to de-differentiate to an ISC state.
claims.source: However, a recent work suggested that RasG12V can push a small number of EBs to de-differentiate to an ISC state (Tian et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to recent work.

claims.claim: The duration of progenitors' cell cycle in RasG12V-expressing lineages was directly measured to be 8±2.76 hr.
claims.source: We directly measured the duration of progenitors' cell cycle in these lineages to be 8±2.76 hr (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Of 17 RasG12V-expressing ISC lineages characterized, one had divisions where both daughter cells from the first recorded division were seen dividing further.
claims.source: Interestingly, of 17 RasG12V-expressing ISC lineages characterized, one had divisions where both daughter cells from the first recorded division were seen dividing further (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: After being generated from an ISC division, enteroendocrine (EE) progenitors are known to divide once to give rise to two mature EEs.
claims.source: For example, after being generated from an ISC division, enteroendocrine (EE) progenitors are also known to divide once to give rise to two mature EEs (Chen et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Co-expression of string (stg) and Cyclin E (CycE) is sufficient to strongly induce ISC proliferation.
claims.source: The combined expression of these two gene products is sufficient to strongly induce ISC proliferation (Kohlmaier et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Stg and CycE have been shown to promote EB mitoses, although much less strongly than in ISCs.
claims.source: Notably, Stg and CycE have also been shown to promote EB mitoses (Kohlmaier et al., 2015), although much less strongly than in ISCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: The fraction of progenitor cells that divided in response to stg and CycE co-expression (~25%) was not significantly different from that observed after forced expression of RasG12V.
claims.source: The fraction of progenitor cells that divided in response to stg and CycE co-expression (~25%; Figure 4D) was not significantly different from that observed after forced expression of RasG12V, suggesting that all receptive progenitors are activated in both cases.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Co-dividing siblings appeared in 6 of 12 ISC lineages that overexpressed stg and CycE.
claims.source: However, co-dividing siblings appeared in 6 of 12 ISC lineages that overexpressed stg and CycE (Figure 4E), a significantly higher frequency to the 1 of 17 observed after RasG12V overexpression (p=0.0106, Fisher's exact test).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4E and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: No significant difference in cell cycle duration was detected in progenitors' cell cycles driven by stg and CycE (9.4±4.6 hr) and cell cycles driven by RasG12V (8±2.76 hr).
claims.source: We detected no significant difference in cell cycle duration in progenitors' cell cycles driven by stg and CycE (9.4±4.6 hr) and cell cycles driven by RasG12V (8±2.76 hr; Figure 4F), suggesting that their differing abilities to produce co-dividing sibling cells may reflect different effects on the differentiation process.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Eight divisions yielded co-dividing siblings.
claims.source: Combining all the lineages described above, we were able to identify eight divisions that yielded co-dividing siblings (see Figure 6A–B and Figure 5—video 1 for an example).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6A-B and Figure 5—video 1.

claims.claim: For seven co-dividing sibling pairs, sibling cells divided within 2 hr of each other.
claims.source: For seven of these, sibling cells divided within 2 hr of each other, while for one pair the interval was 5 hr.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: 17 sibling pairs were classified as non-co-dividing.
claims.source: Following this definition, we classified 17 sibling pairs as non-co-dividing (see Figure 6D–F and Figure 6—video 2 for an example), 9 from RasG12V- and 8 from stg and CycE-expressing guts.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6D-F and Figure 6—video 2.

claims.claim: For 8 of 17 non-co-dividing pairs, the non-dividing cells displayed increases in nuclear size over time and lost GFP expression, which is indicative of differentiation towards the EC cell fate.
claims.source: Interestingly, for 8 of these 17 pairs, the non-dividing cells displayed increases in nuclear size over time, and also lost GFP expression, which is indicative of differentiation towards the EC cell fate (Figure 6C and G–H).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6C and G-H.

claims.claim: Co-dividing siblings increased their nuclear size before dividing further, but maintained GFP expression.
claims.source: This behavior was not observed for co-dividing siblings, where both cells increased their nuclear size before dividing further, but maintained GFP expression (Figure 6A and E–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 6A and E-F.

claims.claim: It was previously reported that spindle orientation is indicative of whether an ISC mitosis is asymmetric or symmetric.
claims.source: It was previously reported that spindle orientation is indicative of whether an ISC mitosis is asymmetric or symmetric, with symmetric divisions being planar relative to the visceral muscle layer, and asymmetric divisions displacing one daughter cell apically, away from the visceral muscle (Hu and Jasper, 2019; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007; Goulas et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous work.

claims.claim: Measured angles between sister cells after mitosis were found to be <15° in 29/33 cases for RasG12V- and in 30/32 cases for stg +CycE-induced mitoses.
claims.source: Measured angles were found to be <15° in 29/33 cases for RasG12V- and in 30/32 cases for stg +CycE-induced mitoses.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental measurements.

claims.claim: No significant differences in sister cell angles were observed between co-dividing and non-co-dividing siblings.
claims.source: Moreover, no significant differences in sister cell angles were observed between co-dividing and non-co-dividing siblings (Figure 7A–C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7A-C.

claims.claim: These observations do not support the view that apical displacement of daughter cells is associated with EB fate specification.
claims.source: These observations do not support that view that apical displacement of daughter cells is associated with EB fate specification.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Cells in non-co-dividing pairs remained close to one another until the following mitotic event.
claims.source: Measuring the distance between sister cells at each time interval, we found that cells in non-co-dividing pairs remained close to one another until the following mitotic event (Figure 7D, red line).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Cells in co-dividing pairs moved apart from one another.
claims.source: Cells in co-dividing pairs, however, moved apart from one another (Figure 7D, green line).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Commitment to differentiation requires that sister cells remain in contact for ~3–5 hr.
claims.source: If co-division and non-co-division are indeed indicative of symmetric and asymmetric division, respectively, this observation suggests that commitment to differentiation, as occurs after asymmetric divisions, requires that sister cells remain in contact for ~3–5 hr (Figure 7D and F, red line).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: This is in line with previous measurements of Notch activation dynamics in differentiating EBs.
claims.source: This is in line with previous measurements of Notch activation dynamics in differentiating EBs (Martin et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Rapid separation of sister cells following a division may be necessary to generate a symmetric division that duplicates ISCs.
claims.source: Conversely, rapid separation of sister cells following a division may be necessary to generate a symmetric division that duplicates ISCs.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The genotype used to induce proliferation did not have an effect on the cell motility of either sibling type.
claims.source: We found that the genotype used to induce proliferation did not have an effect on the cell motility of either sibling type (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: No difference in cell motility was found when considering the effect of time on cell movement of non-co-dividing or co-dividing siblings.
claims.source: Likewise, no difference in cell motility was found when considering the effect of time on cell movement of non-co-dividing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C) or co-dividing (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) siblings.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-D.

claims.claim: No significant difference in cell motility was found when directly comparing both pair types irrespective of genotype or time-point analyzed.
claims.source: Therefore, we directly compared the motility of both pair types irrespective of genotype or time-point analyzed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E), but also found no significant difference.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: Cells of both pair types migrate within the epithelium at similar speeds.
claims.source: This indicates that cells of both pair types migrate within the epithelium at similar speeds.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Since non-co-dividing siblings tend to remain close to one another over time, their movement is most likely random.
claims.source: Since non-co-dividing siblings tend to remain close to one another over time, their movement is most likely random.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: Since the distance between co-dividing siblings increases over time, their movement is likely more directional, such that cells in a sibling pair move away from each other.
claims.source: On the other hand, since the distance between co-dividing siblings increases over time, their movement is likely more directional, such that cells in a sibling pair move away from each other.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: The magnitudes of the reconstructed relative movements between co-dividing pairs was significantly greater than that for non-co-dividing pairs.
claims.source: As expected, the magnitudes of the reconstructed relative movements between co-dividing pairs was significantly greater than that for non-co-dividing pairs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: The movement of co-dividing cell pairs was directional, with the two cells moving away from one another right after division.
claims.source: This confirms that the movement of co-dividing cell pairs was directional, with the two cells moving away from one another right after division.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental observations.

claims.claim: GFP expression could be induced in Malpighian tubules cultured at 18 °C for 24 hr and then shifted to the permissive temperature (29 °C), indicating their long-term survival.
claims.source: Using the esgTS driver system, GFP expression could be induced in tubules cultured at 18 °C for 24 hr and then shifted to the permissive temperature (29 °C), indicating their long-term survival (Figure 8A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8A-B.

claims.claim: Malpighian tubules cultured for 3 days could still contract regularly, albeit only if still attached to intestines.
claims.source: Moreover, we found that Malpighian tubules cultured for 3 days could still contract regularly (Video 2), albeit only if still attached to intestines.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Video 2.

claims.claim: Adult hearts (the dorsal vessel) could be seen still beating regularly after up to 10 days in culture.
claims.source: On closer inspection, we found that adult hearts (the dorsal vessel), which lay along the abdominal cuticle, could be seen still beating regularly after up to 10 days in culture (Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Video 3.

claims.claim: The muscle sheet that envelopes the ovaries still contracted after 3 days in culture.
claims.source: Similarly, the muscle sheet that envelopes the ovaries still contracted after 3 days in culture (Video 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Video 4.

claims.claim: A distinctive characteristic of stage 1–8 follicles is their rotation within their follicle cell sheath, along their long axis.
claims.source: A distinctive characteristic of stage 1–8 follicles is their rotation within their follicle cell sheath, along their long axis (Cetera et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: In ex vivo cultures, rotating stage 4 follicles were routinely observed that grew in size and started to elongate, indicative of progression to stage 5.
claims.source: In our ex vivo cultures, we routinely observed rotating stage 4 follicles that grew in size and started to elongate (Figure 8C–C' and Figure 8—video 1), indicative of progression to stage 5 (Cetera et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by data in Figure 8C-C' and Figure 8—video 1, as well as a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Follicle rotation continued for up to 48 hr, suggesting the long-term survival of follicles in the explants.
claims.source: Notably, this phenomenon continued for up to 48 hr, suggesting the long-term survival of follicles in our explants.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the results section based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Currently available Drosophila culture media are based on larval hemolymph composition.
claims.source: Firstly, currently available Drosophila culture media are based on larval hemolymph composition.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as background knowledge.

claims.claim: Minimal modifications to Schneider's medium are sufficient to reduce cell death ex vivo.
claims.source: We have shown here that minimal modifications to Schneider's medium are sufficient to reduce cell death ex vivo (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Midguts may receive nutrients and signaling molecules from other organs such as ovaries and fat body, which are in close proximity to the intestine.
claims.source: Midguts may also receive nutrients and signaling molecules from other organs such as ovaries and fat body, which are in close proximity to the intestine.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section as a hypothesis.

claims.claim: Using fly extract as a culture medium and co-culturing intestines with ovaries and fly abdomens resulted in dramatic decreases in cell death.
claims.source: Indeed, using fly extract as a culture medium and co-culturing intestines with ovaries and fly abdomens resulted in dramatic decreases in cell death (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by data in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Proper oxygenation is a concern as it had been found to be essential for other Drosophila organ ex vivo cultures.
claims.source: Proper oxygenation is also a concern as it had been found to be essential for other Drosophila organ ex vivo cultures (Strassburger et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Trachea ramify throughout the fly's internal organs, and in the intestine they even reach through the visceral muscle to contact epithelial cells directly.
claims.source: Indeed, trachea ramify throughout the fly's internal organs, and in the intestine they even reach through the visceral muscle to contact epithelial cells directly (Li et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the discussion section and supported by a citation to previous work.

claims.claim: Prolonged live-imaging sessions can be hampered by phototoxicity.

results.result: The authors developed an improved organ explant culture protocol for adult Drosophila midguts that extends viability from <16 hours to up to 3 days ex vivo. This was achieved through optimized dissection technique, modified culture medium with increased Na+/K+ ratio and trehalose concentration mimicking adult hemolymph, air-liquid interface culture for enhanced oxygenation, and addition of antioxidants and calcium blocker isradipine.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C4, C16-C31, C109, C111 collectively demonstrate the development and validation of the extended culture protocol. The dissection technique (C16-C17), medium modifications (C3, C20-C25), air-liquid interface setup (C4, C18-C19), and additives (C26-C31) are all supported by experimental data in Figure 2A showing reduced cell death. The improvement over previous <16 hour protocols (C1) is well-documented with citations.

results.result: Progenitor cells (ISCs and EBs) are quiescent in healthy explanted midguts, showing no proliferation, stable GFP expression, and constant nuclear size for up to 48-72 hours. This quiescence is attributed to the absence of cell death and the proliferation-suppressive effect of healthy enterocytes.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 provide direct observational evidence from live imaging (Figure 3A, 3D, F, G, Figure 4) showing no division, stable markers, and constant nuclear size in healthy explants. Claims C37-C38, C49-C52, C117-C118 provide mechanistic context supported by citations to prior work. The observation that damage can activate progenitors (C52) validates that the cells remain competent, strengthening the quiescence conclusion.

results.result: Midgut progenitor cells can respond to tissue damage ex vivo by proliferating and differentiating to replace lost cells. This was demonstrated using SDS feeding and mechanical wounding protocols, with progenitor cells showing nuclear enlargement, loss of GFP expression indicative of differentiation, and occasional proliferation events, particularly at later timepoints (48hr) and in extensively damaged regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C40-C48 are supported by extensive live-imaging data (Figure 3B-C, E-G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1-2) showing progenitor cell responses to damage. The differentiation events (nuclear enlargement, GFP loss) are well-documented, and proliferation is observed in damaged regions. The in vivo validation (C44-C46) strengthens the findings. The temporal pattern (proliferation mainly at 48hr) is consistent across methods.

results.result: Notch signaling remains functional ex vivo, as demonstrated by Notch RNAi experiments showing that N-depleted progenitor cells require tissue damage to proliferate and fail to differentiate when they do proliferate, consistent with in vivo tumor formation requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C58 demonstrate functional Notch signaling ex vivo. The requirement for damage to induce proliferation in N-depleted cells (C56-C57) and the block in differentiation (C58) are supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and videos. This recapitulates known in vivo behavior (C54-C55), validating the culture system's ability to maintain key signaling pathways.

results.result: Temperature-sensitive gene induction is functional ex vivo, enabling genetic stimulation of progenitor proliferation through RasG12V or stg/CycE co-expression. Both approaches induced proliferation in ~20-25% of progenitor cells with similar cell cycle durations (8±2.76 hr for RasG12V, 9.4±4.6 hr for stg/CycE), allowing tracking of cells through multiple divisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C59-C68, C71, C74-C76, C78 are supported by extensive live-imaging data (Figure 4, Figure 5). The temperature-sensitive system works ex vivo, both genetic manipulations induce proliferation at similar rates (C76), and cell cycle durations are directly measured (C71, C78). The ability to track multiple divisions (C67-C68) demonstrates the extended imaging capability. Data in Figure 4D-F support the quantitative claims.

results.result: Extended live imaging enabled reconstruction of 17 RasG12V-expressing and 12 stg/CycE-expressing ISC lineages through multiple divisions. RasG12V stimulation predominantly produced non-co-dividing siblings (16/17 lineages), while stg/CycE produced co-dividing siblings more frequently (6/12 lineages, p=0.0106). Non-co-dividing siblings showed differentiation markers (nuclear enlargement, GFP loss in 8/17 pairs), while co-dividing siblings maintained GFP expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C69-C70, C72-C73, C77, C79-C83, C128-C129 are supported by detailed lineage analysis (Figure 5, Figure 6). The statistical difference in co-dividing sibling frequency between RasG12V and stg/CycE is significant (C77, p=0.0106). The differentiation markers in non-co-dividing pairs (C82) and their absence in co-dividing pairs (C83) are documented in Figure 6C, E-H. The interpretation that founding cells are likely ISCs (C69) is reasonable given prior knowledge (C69, C73).

results.result: Sister cell angles after mitosis were predominantly <15° (29/33 for RasG12V, 30/32 for stg/CycE) with no significant differences between co-dividing and non-co-dividing siblings, contradicting the hypothesis that apical displacement of daughter cells is associated with EB fate specification.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by quantitative measurements (Figure 7A-C). The lack of difference in sister cell angles between co-dividing and non-co-dividing pairs (C86) directly contradicts prior hypotheses about spindle orientation and fate (C84, C87). However, the authors acknowledge they did not directly measure spindle orientation during mitosis, which is a limitation. The conclusion (C87) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Co-dividing and non-co-dividing sibling pairs show distinct spatial behaviors: non-co-dividing siblings remain close together (~3-5 hr), while co-dividing siblings actively move apart. Both cell types have similar motility speeds, but co-dividing pairs show significantly greater relative movement, indicating directional separation. This suggests that sustained cell-cell contact (~3-5 hr) may be required for differentiation commitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C100 are supported by detailed tracking analysis (Figure 7D-F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The distance measurements (C88-C89) show clear differences between pair types (Figure 7D). The motility analysis (C93-C96) demonstrates similar speeds but different movement patterns. The relative movement analysis (C99-C100) confirms directional separation in co-dividing pairs. The inference about contact duration and differentiation (C90) is reasonable and consistent with prior Notch dynamics data (C91).

results.result: The culture system supports Malpighian tubules for up to 3 days, with temperature-sensitive GFP induction functional and tubules capable of regular contractions when attached to intestines.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C101-C102 are supported by data in Figure 8A-B and Video 2. GFP induction in tubules demonstrates long-term viability and functional gene expression. The requirement for intestinal attachment for contractions (C102) is an interesting observation but not fully explained.

results.result: Ovaries can be cultured for up to 3 days with the muscle sheet remaining contractile. Stage 4 follicles show characteristic rotation and growth, progressing to stage 5 over 48 hours, indicating long-term viability and developmental progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C104-C107 are supported by data in Figure 8C-C', Figure 8—video 1, and Video 4. The observation of follicle rotation (C105-C106), a well-characterized developmental process, for up to 48 hours (C107) demonstrates functional culture. The muscle contractions (C104) provide additional evidence of viability.

results.result: Adult hearts (dorsal vessel) can be cultured and maintain regular beating for up to 10 days, with the visceral muscle also surviving up to a week in optimal conditions despite adjacent epithelial death.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C103, C144 are supported by Video 3 and observational data. The 10-day heart survival is remarkable and represents the longest culture duration reported. The observation that visceral muscle survives longer than epithelium (C144) suggests differential sensitivity to culture conditions, possibly related to bacterial growth in the lumen.

results.result: The authors discuss limitations of the culture system including: dissection-induced damage risk, agarose pad interference with high-power objectives, bacterial growth limiting survival, phototoxicity concerns, and potential negative effects of suppressing peristalsis. They propose potential improvements including thinner agarose pads with increased oxygen, axenic flies, light-sheet microscopy, and organ-specific media optimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C108, C110, C112-C115, C139-C152 represent honest assessment of limitations and speculation about improvements. The limitations are well-documented (bacterial growth in C143-C144, dissection challenges in C139, optical limitations in C140). The proposed solutions (C141-C142, C145-C146) are reasonable but speculative. This critical self-assessment strengthens the overall work.

results.result: The authors propose that enteroblasts are a stable cell type rather than transient progenitors, potentially serving as a first-line response to damage. They suggest the EGFR-Ras-Erk pathway may have a role in differentiation, while stg/CycE may suppress differentiation. They hypothesize that cell-cell contacts mediated by adherens junctions are required for differentiation, and that co-dividing siblings resulting from symmetric divisions may disperse to space ISCs uniformly in the epithelium.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C121, C127, C130-C138 represent interpretations and hypotheses based on the data. While the observations supporting these ideas are sound (stable EB markers, differential effects of RasG12V vs stg/CycE, cell movement patterns), the mechanistic conclusions are speculative. The EB stability hypothesis (C119-C121) is reasonable but lacks direct lineage tracing with differentiation markers. The pathway interpretations (C130-C131) and adherens junction role (C135-C136) are plausible but not directly tested. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work rather than established conclusions.

results.result: The manuscript includes numerous claims about prior work and general knowledge regarding Drosophila intestinal stem cell biology, hemolymph composition, signaling pathways, and other biological processes. These claims are supported by appropriate citations to the literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C15, C21, C37, C50-C51, C53-C55, C59-C61, C69, C73-C75, C84, C105, C116, C120, C122-C126, C132-C136, C138, C148, C151 represent background knowledge and prior work. All are appropriately cited and accurately represent the referenced literature. These provide essential context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that their protocol enables extended survival and live imaging of Drosophila organs ex vivo, providing a platform for studying epithelial homeostasis, inter-organ interactions, and real-time effects of gene manipulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C155 represent appropriate conclusions based on the demonstrated capabilities of the system. The extended survival (C153) is well-documented, the potential for studying inter-organ interactions (C154) is supported by the co-culture data, and the utility for gene manipulation studies (C155) is demonstrated by the temperature-sensitive experiments. These are reasonable assessments of the system's capabilities and potential applications.
